children.label: Download & import
children.summary: Downloads EnterpriseRAG-Bench from Hugging Face and loads its 512K documents and 500 questions into Postgres.
children.details:
Produces the `documents` and `questions` Postgres tables that every later module (parsing, indexing, retrieval, evaluation) reads from. It is the first step of the pipeline and is run once per machine.

Flow:
- `download_dataset` pulls the dataset card and parquet files from Hugging Face into `data/enterprise_rag_bench`.
- `EnterpriseRagBenchLoader.load` reads `data/documents/test.parquet` and `data/questions/test.parquet` into a `Corpus` of `Artifact` and `Question` models.
- `import_corpus` converts them to `DocumentRecord` and `QuestionRecord` rows, creates the tables, and inserts through the repository layer in batches of 2000.
- It prints per-source document counts and the question count as a sanity check.

Commands are `train-rag download`, `import-db` and `setup` (both), wired in `main.py`. Read `import_db.py` first, then the loader.

children.label: DataLoader
children.summary: ABC that turns any data source into a normalized Corpus.
children.details:
The contract is one abstract method, `load() -> Corpus`, plus a class attribute `name` that identifies the dataset.

The `name` is stored as the `dataset` column on every row, so several datasets can share the same tables. A new variant must set `name` and implement `load()`; it owns all knowledge of where the data lives and how it is shaped, and returns `Artifact` and `Question` models. Nothing downstream of the loader sees the raw format.

children.label: Strategy loader
children.summary: Importers depend only on Corpus, so a new dataset needs just a new DataLoader subclass.
children.details: Strategy pattern. `base.py` says it directly: "the rest of the pipeline only ever sees `Corpus`". `import_corpus` in `import_db.py` calls `loader.load()` and then uses `loader.name` and `corpus.artifacts` / `corpus.questions`, never parquet or Hugging Face types. Today only `EnterpriseRagBenchLoader` exists, and `import_corpus` instantiates it directly, so swapping the dataset still needs a small edit there.

children.label: EnterpriseRagBenchLoader
children.summary: Reads documents and questions from local parquet files, optionally filtered by source.
children.details:
The only `DataLoader` subclass, with `name = "enterprise_rag_bench"`. The constructor takes `data_dir` and an optional list of `SourceType`s.

- `load_artifacts` reads `data/documents/test.parquet` with pyarrow, appends a `row_index` column (0-based position in the file), filters on `source_type` when `source_types` is set, and builds one `Artifact` per row from `doc_id`, `source_type`, `title` and `content`.
- `load_questions` reads `data/questions/test.parquet` into `Question` models (gold answer, answer facts, expected doc ids). Questions are never filtered by source.
- `resolve` raises `FileNotFoundError` with a hint to run `train-rag download` when a file is missing.

The row_index is taken before filtering, so it always points at the original parquet row. The full table is loaded through `to_pylist`, which is fine for the benchmark's size.

children.label: Rerunnable import
children.summary: Batched commits with on-conflict-do-nothing inserts let an interrupted import be rerun safely.
children.details: `insert_documents` uses Postgres `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` on (`dataset`, `source_file`, `row_index`), and `insert_questions` does the same on the question `id`. Each batch of 2000 is committed on its own, so a crash loses at most one batch and a rerun skips what is already stored and fills in the rest.

children.summary: NUL characters are written as the visible text \x00 because Postgres text cannot store them.
children.details: `escape_nul` replaces "\x00" with the four visible characters `\x00`. Its docstring gives the reason for escaping instead of deleting: a few documents mention a NUL delimiter literally, so the escape keeps their meaning. Only title and content are escaped; question text is not.

children.summary: Documents live in Postgres so later steps query them instead of rereading parquet.
children.details: The article says: "I put the whole corpus into Postgres first, with each document's source, size and origin. That way every later step can query it, instead of me rereading parquet files." The corpus is 511,962 documents from nine tools plus 500 questions. Storing `char_count`, `byte_size`, `source_type` and provenance at import time lets size analysis run as SQL and lets parsed documents link back to their raw row.

children.summary: main.py runs setup as download then import-db, sharing both steps with their own commands.
children.details: In `main.py`, `if args.command in ("download", "setup")` runs `download_dataset`, and the next `if args.command in ("import-db", "setup")` runs `import_corpus`. Both read the same `--data-dir`. So `setup` has no code of its own: it is the two steps in sequence.

children.label: Parsing per source
children.summary: Deterministic, LLM-free parsers turn each source's raw documents into typed pydantic models.
children.details:
Produces one `ParsedDocument` per raw document for seven sources (Slack, Gmail, Linear, HubSpot, Fireflies, GitHub, Jira), for the chunking and retrieval steps that need channel, participants, dates and clean sections. Google Drive and Confluence have no parser.

Flow:
- `parse_documents` (processing/parsing.py) converts each stored `DocumentRecord` with `to_artifact` and hands it to `ParserRegistry.parse`.
- The registry picks the parser by `SourceType`; the parser normalises newlines, tries one method per field format via `try_formats`, and builds a typed model.
- A document in no known format comes back as `OpenText`.
- `upsert_parsed_documents` stores the model as JSONB in the `parsed_documents` table, next to the raw text.

In the article's final tally every document of the seven sources is a typed model or open text, with 0 flagged. Read `parsers/base.py` first, then `slack.py` as the largest worked example.

children.label: DocumentParser
children.summary: ABC with parse(), try_formats, missing_fields and an open-text fallback.
children.details:
The contract every parser shares, in `DocumentParser[ParsedT]`:
- `source_type`: ClassVar naming the source it handles.
- `parse(artifact)` (abstract): returns the typed model or `OpenText`; never raises on malformed input.
- `try_formats(field, source, extractors, formats)`: runs one method per format in order, records the winning method's name in `formats[field]`, returns the first non-empty value or None.
- `missing(**fields)`: names of expected fields that are None, empty string or empty list; the result goes into `missing_fields`, which makes `ParsedDocument.flagged` true.
- `open_text(artifact)`: whole text as `OpenText`, `useful=False` under `MIN_USEFUL_CHARS` (300).

A new source needs a `DocumentParser` subclass with `source_type` and `parse`, a `ParsedDocument` subclass in models/parsed, and registration in `ParserRegistry`. A new format for an existing field is one extra method added to the extractor list.

children.label: base.py
children.summary: DocumentParser with try_formats, missing and open_text.
children.details: Generic over the parsed model (`class DocumentParser[ParsedT: ParsedDocument](ABC)`). `try_formats` is a static generic: it loops over extractors, and the first truthy value wins and writes `extractor.__name__` into the `formats` dict. `open_text` normalises newlines, strips, and sets `useful` from the 300-char threshold.

outline.name: DocumentParser
outline.doc:
Parse one source's raw documents into structured fields, without an LLM.

Subclasses handle a single source type. A parser never raises on a malformed
document: it returns what it could parse and lists the expected fields it could
not find in `missing_fields`, so the document can be reviewed later.

When a field is written in several formats, the parser has one method per format
and tries them in order with `try_formats`; to support a new format, add a method
and put it in that list. A document in none of the formats is returned as
`OpenText` by `open_text`.

children.name: parse
children.doc:
Parse one document.

Args:
    artifact: Raw document of this parser's source type.

Returns:
    The parsed fields and the expected fields that are missing, or the whole
    document as open text when it is in none of the formats.

children.name: open_text
children.doc:
Keep a document in none of the formats as one block of open text.

Args:
    artifact: Raw document.

Returns:
    The whole text; not useful when under `MIN_USEFUL_CHARS` characters.

children.name: missing
children.doc:
List the names of expected fields that are empty.

Args:

Returns:

children.name: try_formats
children.signature: (field: str, source: InputT, extractors: Sequence[Callable[[InputT], ValueT | None]], formats: dict[str, str]) -> ValueT | None
children.doc:
Try one method per format, in order, until one finds the field.

Args:
    field: Name of the field being extracted.
    source: What the methods read: the title, the content or its sections.
    extractors: Format methods; each returns the value, or None or an empty
        value when the document is not in its format.
    formats: Format used per field; the winning method's name is recorded here.

Returns:
    The first value found, or None when no format matches.

children.details: `ParsedDocument` carries `doc_id`, `source_type`, `document_id` (the Postgres row id, needed because the dataset reuses a few `doc_id`s), `formats`, `missing_fields` and `useful`. outline.name: ParsedDocument
outline.doc:

A document with missing fields is flagged for review instead of failing the run.
`document_id` links back to the raw document (title and content) in the Postgres
`documents` table; `doc_id` alone is not enough, as the dataset reuses a few ids.

children.details: A `ParsedDocument` with a single `text` field. Per the article, open text gives every unstructured document the same preprocessing instead of per-source special cases. Counts: Jira 370, Fireflies 131, Gmail 30, Slack 24, Linear 13, GitHub 1.

outline.name: OpenText
outline.doc:
A document in none of its source's formats, kept as one block of open text.

Every parser falls back to it the same way, so these documents get the same
preprocessing later whatever their source. It is never flagged: there are no
fields to miss. Text under `MIN_USEFUL_CHARS` characters is marked not useful.

children.label: Format methods tried in order
children.summary: One method per field format, tried in order by try_formats; the winner is recorded in formats.
children.details: When a field can be written several ways (a Slack channel from title or path, a Fireflies date from six header layouts), the parser has one small method per format and lists them in order. `try_formats` records which method won in `ParsedDocument.formats`, e.g. `{"channel": "channel_from_path"}`. That makes it possible to count how often each format occurs and to support a new one by adding one method to the list. The article introduced this after a parser handling only the most common layout missed many documents.
children.doc: docs/articles/001_data_exploration_and_parsing.md

children.label: Parsers never raise
children.summary: Missing expected fields are listed so documents can be flagged and reviewed, not crash a 500K run.
children.details: Parsers return whatever they found and list absent expected fields in `missing_fields` (built with `missing()`). Over roughly 480K documents a raised exception would stop the run; a flag lets the documents be read later to decide whether the data is truly missing or the parser is wrong. The article reports 0 flagged documents at the end, after fixes and LLM helpers for Slack messages, Fireflies dates and attendees.
children.doc: docs/articles/001_data_exploration_and_parsing.md

children.label: Open text fallback
children.summary: A document in no known format becomes OpenText; under 300 chars it is marked not useful.
children.details: `open_text` uses `MIN_USEFUL_CHARS = 300` from parsers/text.py. A not-useful document is not flagged, since there is nothing left to review, but it is not worth embedding. Of 569 open-text documents only 35 are not useful (Slack 23, Gmail 8, Fireflies 3, Jira 1); Gmail also routes any whole thread under 300 characters here.
children.doc: docs/articles/001_data_exploration_and_parsing.md

children.label: Slack
children.summary: Splits a thread into speaker-line messages and recovers the channel from title or path.
children.details:
Handles 285,605 threads, the biggest source. Differs from the others by two multi-format fields: `channel` (`channel_from_title` accepts only the 34 `KNOWN_CHANNELS`, then `channel_from_path` reads `slack/<channel>/`) and `messages` (strict speaker lines, Python list, loose speaker lines, bracketed `[name]:`, braced `{name}:`).

A thread with no channel becomes `chat_type="group_chat"`, not flagged: an LLM judge found a channel in only 0.4% of a 956-thread sample of the 9,043 channel-less threads. The constructor takes `inferred_messages` (LLM-split messages by document id) that override the regex result with format `messages_inferred`. No messages means open text.

children.label: slack.py
children.summary: SlackParser: channel from title or path, then message splitting in five formats.
children.details: `parse` runs `try_formats` for `channel` and `messages`, applies LLM-inferred messages if present, and builds a `SlackThread` with `thread_starter` (first message) and unique `participants`. `KNOWN_CHANNELS` holds the 34 channels; `CHANNEL_IN_PATH` matches leaked file paths.

outline.name: SlackParser
outline.doc:
Parse a Slack thread: one `speaker: text` or `Name (Role): text` line per message.

The title is the channel name when it is one of the workspace's channels. Other
titles are leaked file paths, where the channel is recovered from
`slack/<channel>/...` when present, or numbers, sentences and one-off slugs. A
thread with no channel is labelled a group chat rather than flagged. A thread with
no messages in any format is kept as open text. When an LLM split the thread into
messages (several messages on one line, or code lines taken for speakers), that split
is used instead, with the format `messages_inferred`.

children.name: __init__
children.signature: (self, inferred_messages: Mapping[int, list[SlackMessage]] | None = None) -> None
children.doc:
Set up the parser.

Args:
    inferred_messages: Messages an LLM split, keyed by document id, from
        `load_inferred_messages`; None when they are not loaded.

children.name: parse
children.doc:
Parse one Slack thread.

Args:
    artifact: Raw Slack document.

Returns:
    The thread with its channel, starter, participants and messages.

children.name: channel_from_title
children.doc:
Format 1: the title is the channel name.

Only `KNOWN_CHANNELS` count: the names used as the title of at least 7 threads.
Titles that are numbers (`2112233445`), sentences, document ids or one-off topic
slugs (`compact-cta-toast-ordering`) are not channels.

Args:
    title: Document title.

Returns:
    The channel name, or None when the title is not a known channel.

children.name: channel_from_path
children.doc:
Format 2: the title is a leaked file path like `slack/<channel>/...`.

Args:
    title: Document title.

Returns:
    The channel name, or None when the path has no channel.

children.name: messages_from_speaker_lines
children.doc:
Format 1: one `speaker: text` or `Name (Role): text` line per message.

Lines written the looser way of format 3 (` dave_oncall:`, `maria gonzalez:`)
also start a message when the speaker's first name is a known one; see
`known_speaker_line`.

Args:
    content: Raw thread text.

Returns:
    The messages in order, or None when no line starts with a speaker.

children.name: messages_from_python_list
children.doc:
Format 2: the thread is a Python list of `speaker: text` strings.

Args:
    content: Raw thread text; decoded before newlines are normalized, since
        the list's strings hold escaped line breaks.

Returns:
    The messages in order, or None when the content is not such a list.

children.name: messages_from_loose_speaker_lines
children.doc:
Format 3: looser speaker lines than format 1.

Lines may start with spaces, full names may be lowercase (`maria gonzalez:`),
and roles may follow without a space (`rebecca(auditor):`) or after a dash
(`maria - Sales:`).

Args:
    content: Raw thread text.

Returns:
    The messages in order, or None when no line starts with a speaker.

children.name: messages_from_bracketed_speakers
children.doc:
Format 4: `[alex] 1789456789: text`, a bracketed speaker and a Unix timestamp.

The timestamp is optional (`[alex]: text`) and is not kept.

Args:
    content: Raw thread text.

Returns:
    The messages in order, or None when no line starts with a bracketed speaker.

children.name: messages_from_braced_speakers
children.doc:
Format 5: `{Rosie}: text`, a speaker in curly braces.

Args:
    content: Raw thread text.

Returns:
    The messages in order, or None when no line starts with a braced speaker.

children.label: speakers.py
children.summary: Speaker-line regexes and known first names to tell speakers from code keys.
children.details: Regexes `SPEAKER_LINE` (strict, `Name (Role):`), `LOOSE_SPEAKER_LINE`, `BRACKETED_SPEAKER_LINE`, `BRACED_SPEAKER_LINE`. `known_speaker_line` accepts a loose match only if the first name of the handle (split on `_ . -`, after joining names broken by a stray space) is in `KNOWN_FIRST_NAMES` or the speaker ends in `bot`. `speaker_messages` builds `SlackMessage`s, appending non-speaker lines to the previous message.

outline.name: known_speaker_line
outline.doc:
Match a strict speaker line, or a loose one from a known person or a bot.

Code blocks hold `name:` and `enabled:` lines that look like loose speaker lines;
the first name of the speaker (`dave` in `dave_oncall`) tells them apart. Names
split by a stray space (`ev an`, `mar ia`) are joined before the lookup, and
speakers ending in `bot` (`deploy-bot`) count too.

Args:
    line: One thread line.

Returns:
    The match, or None when the line does not start a message.

outline.name: strict_speaker_messages
outline.doc:
Split lines into messages when at least one line is a strict speaker line.

Args:
    lines: Thread lines.

Returns:
    The messages in order, or None when no line strictly starts with a speaker, so
    that the looser formats are tried.

outline.name: speaker_messages
outline.doc:
Split lines into messages; lines without a speaker continue the previous one.

Args:
    lines: Thread lines.
    speaker_line: Match of a line that starts a message, with `speaker`, `text`
        and optional `role` or `dash_role` groups.

Returns:
    The messages in order.

children.label: slack.py (model)
children.summary: SlackThread and SlackMessage.
children.details: `SlackMessage` is speaker (None if unknown), role and text. `SlackThread` adds `channel`, `chat_type` (`channel` or `group_chat`), `thread_starter`, `participants` and `messages`.

outline.name: SlackMessage
outline.doc: One message of a thread; `speaker` is None when the sender is unknown.

outline.name: SlackThread
outline.doc:
A Slack thread with its channel and participants.

`chat_type` is `group_chat` for a thread with no channel: neither its title nor its
text names one. These read as short-lived group chats set up to resolve one issue;
an LLM judge on a random sample of 956 of them found the channel in only 0.4%, so a
missing channel is a label, not something to review.

children.label: Known first names
children.summary: Thread-starter first names separate speaker lines like dave_oncall: from config key: lines in code blocks.
children.details: A looser speaker pattern would split messages correctly but also treat `name:` or `enabled:` lines in pasted code as speakers. So loose lines count only when the speaker's first name is in `KNOWN_FIRST_NAMES` (taken from thread starters) or the speaker is a bot. See `known_speaker_line` in parsers/speakers.py; the article's last section covers this trade-off.
children.doc: docs/articles/001_data_exploration_and_parsing.md

children.label: Fireflies
children.summary: Meeting transcripts: summary required, header date and attendees tried in many layouts.
children.details:
10,173 meetings. The summary is required: without a Fireflies summary the document is open text (131 of them). Three multi-format fields: `content` (Python list or plain text), `held_on` (six date methods over header layouts), `attendees` (labeled, unlabeled list, or transcript speakers).

Two LLM outputs fill gaps without overwriting parsed data: `held_on_inferred` (an `InferredDate` with precision and evidence) when the header has no date, and `attendees_inferred` when no attendees are found. Only the attendee gap is flagged, and only when neither source has anyone.

children.label: fireflies.py
children.summary: FirefliesParser: header formats, six date methods and three attendee methods.
children.details: Biggest parser (465 lines). Fields are matched as labels at the start of a line anywhere in the document, since transcript lines begin with a timestamp or speaker. Helpers `labeled_block`, `header_field`, `attendee_text` and `topics` pull the summary, start time, duration and topics. `__init__` takes `inferred_dates` and `inferred_attendees` maps keyed by document id.

outline.name: FirefliesParser
outline.doc:
Parse a meeting: the Fireflies summary, topics and header fields.

The header appears either as one `Meeting header: Date: ...; Start: ...;
Duration: ...; Attendees: ...` line or as separate `Date:`, `Attendees:` lines,
and sometimes sits inside the `transcript:` section. Fields are matched as labels
at the start of a line anywhere in the document; transcript lines start with a
timestamp or speaker, so they do not collide.

A meeting without a Fireflies summary is kept as open text. When the header has no
date, the date an LLM judge estimated from the text is attached as
`held_on_inferred`; a meeting with neither keeps no date and is not flagged, since
there is nothing left to recover it from. When no attendee list or transcript
speaker is found, the speakers an LLM listed are attached as `attendees_inferred`;
only a meeting with neither is flagged.

children.name: __init__
children.signature: (self, inferred_dates: Mapping[int, InferredDate] | None = None, inferred_attendees: Mapping[int, list[Person]] | None = None) -> None
children.doc:
Set up the parser.

Args:
    inferred_dates: Estimated meeting dates keyed by document id, from
        `load_inferred_dates`; None when they are not loaded.
    inferred_attendees: Speakers an LLM listed, keyed by document id, from
        `load_inferred_attendees`; None when they are not loaded.

children.name: parse
children.doc:
Parse one meeting.

Args:
    artifact: Raw Fireflies document.

Returns:
    The meeting with summary, topics, attendees, date, start time and duration,
    or the whole text as open text when there is no summary.

children.name: date_from_date_field
children.doc:
Format 1: a `Date:` or `Date/Time:` field, on its own line or in a `;`/`|` list.

Args:
    header: Normalized meeting text.

Returns:
    The meeting date and time, or None when there is no readable date field.

children.name: date_from_meeting_header
children.doc:
Format 2: a `Meeting header:` line that starts with an unlabeled date.

Args:
    header: Normalized meeting text.

Returns:
    The meeting date and time, or None when there is no such line.

children.name: date_from_header_line
children.doc:
Date format 3: a `Header: 2026-11-04 15:30 UTC | Duration ...` line.

Args:
    header: Normalized meeting text.

Returns:
    The meeting date and time, or None when there is no such line.

children.name: date_from_header_without_colon
children.doc:
Date format 4: `[Meeting header] 2025-03-03 ...` or `Meeting header - 2027-05-04 ...`.

Args:
    header: Normalized meeting text.

Returns:
    The meeting date and time, or None when there is no such line.

children.name: date_from_recorded_field
children.doc:
Date format 5: a `Recorded:` or `Recorded at:` field.

Args:
    header: Normalized meeting text.

Returns:
    The recording date and time, or None when there is no readable field.

children.name: date_from_start_field
children.doc:
Date format 6: a `Meeting start:` or `When:` field.

Args:
    header: Normalized meeting text.

Returns:
    The meeting date and time, or None when there is no readable field.

children.name: content_from_python_list
children.doc:
Content format 1: the meeting is a Python list of strings, one part each.

Args:
    content: Raw meeting content.

Returns:
    The parts joined by line breaks, or None when the content is not such a list.

children.name: content_from_text
children.doc:
Content format 2: plain text, the usual case.

Args:
    content: Raw meeting content.

Returns:
    The text with real line breaks, or None when it is empty.

children.name: attendees_from_labels
children.doc:
Attendees format 1: `Attendees:` lists, inline or on the lines below.

Args:
    header: Normalized meeting text.

Returns:
    The attendees, or None when there is no labeled list.

children.name: attendees_from_unlabeled_list
children.doc:
Attendees format 2: an `Attendees` line with no colon, then one line per group.

Groups look like `Redwood Inference: Ann (AE), Bob` or `- Ann (Redwood)`.

Args:
    header: Normalized meeting text.

Returns:
    The attendees, or None when there is no such list.

children.name: attendees_from_transcript
children.doc:
Attendees format 3: the speakers of `[00:12] Name (Role): ...` transcript lines.

Used when the meeting has no attendee list. Only people who spoke are found;
placeholders like `Speaker 5`, `Note`, `All` or `Host` and bots are skipped.

Args:
    header: Normalized meeting text.

Returns:
    Each speaker once, with the first role given, or None when no line matches.

outline.name: meeting_header_line
outline.doc:
Read the `Meeting header:` line, which can start with an unlabeled date.

Args:
    header: Normalized meeting text.

Returns:
    The line after the label, or None when there is no such line.

outline.name: header_field
outline.doc:
Read a short header field such as `Date: 2027-07-23`.

Args:
    header: Normalized meeting text.
    labels: Alternative labels, separated by `|`.

Returns:
    The field value up to the next `;`, `|` or line break, or up to a sentence
    that starts another field (`~46 minutes. Attendees: ...`); None when absent.

outline.name: attendee_text
outline.doc:
Read every attendee list, e.g. `Attendees (Redwood): ...` and `Attendees (Acme): ...`.

A list is inline after the label, or on the lines below it (bulleted or not).

Args:
    header: Normalized meeting text.

Returns:
    All attendee lists joined by commas, or an empty string when absent.

outline.name: labeled_block
outline.doc:
Read a multi-line block that starts at a label and ends at a blank line or label.

A transcript line (`[00:00] Name: ...`) also ends the block, for meetings without a
`transcript:` key; a summary written as an agenda (`0:05 - Discussed ...`) does not.

Args:
    header: Normalized meeting text.
    label: Pattern of the label line, with an optional `inline` group for
        same-line text.

Returns:
    The block text, or None when the label is absent or empty.

outline.name: is_transcript_line
outline.doc:
Tell whether a line is a transcript line: `[00:00] ...` or `00:00 Name: ...`.

Args:
    line: One line of the meeting.

Returns:
    True when the line starts with a bracketed timestamp or a timestamped speaker.

outline.name: topics
outline.doc:
Read the topics, separated inline by `;` or `,`, or listed one per line.

Args:
    header: Normalized meeting text.

Returns:
    The topics in order.

children.label: fireflies.py (model)
children.summary: FirefliesMeeting and InferredDate.
children.details: `FirefliesMeeting` has summary, topics, attendees, `attendees_inferred`, `held_on`, `held_on_inferred`, start_time and duration. `InferredDate` stores the LLM's date, `precision` (day, week, month), the quoted `evidence` and `year_in_evidence`; inferred is kept apart from parsed so retrieval can decide how far to trust it.

outline.name: InferredDate
outline.doc:
A meeting date estimated by an LLM judge from clues in the text, not read from a header.

`precision` says how close it is: "day" when the text pins the day, "week" for
estimates such as shortly before the earliest action item due date. When
`year_in_evidence` is False the quoted clue has no year, so the year may be a guess.

outline.name: FirefliesMeeting
outline.doc:
A meeting with the summary and header data Fireflies already provides.

`held_on` is the date read from the header. When there is none, `held_on_inferred`
holds the date the LLM judge estimated from the text, if it found one. Likewise
`attendees_inferred` holds the speakers an LLM listed when the text has no attendee
list or speaker lines the parser recognizes.

children.label: Gmail
children.summary: Email threads split into messages with sender, recipients, subject and attachments.
children.details:
121,390 threads. Short-circuits to open text when the content is under 300 characters or no messages are found. The `messages` field has four formats (JSON list, Python list, numbered `message_N_body` sections, text split at `From:` lines). If the text is not numbered and no message has any header, it is open text.

Thread metadata (subject from the first message that has one, participants from senders, recipients and Cc, attachment file names) is derived from the messages. Missing sender, recipients or subject are flagged, except for numbered sections, which carry no headers.

children.label: gmail.py
children.summary: GmailParser: four message-split formats, header parsing, attachment names.
children.details: `message(raw)` parses `HEADER` lines (From, To, Cc, Date, Subject) and the body; helpers `split_addresses`, `attachment_names` (regexes `ATTACHMENTS`, `BULLET`, `FILE_NAME`) and `string_list` support it. Format methods: `messages_from_json_list`, `messages_from_python_list`, `messages_from_numbered_sections`, `messages_from_text`.

outline.name: GmailParser
outline.doc:
Parse a Gmail thread stored as a list of emails, or as plain text.

Most threads are a Python or JSON list of email strings; the rest are plain text
where each email starts at a `From:` line. A thread under `MIN_USEFUL_CHARS`
characters, with no `From:` line, or whose list items are bare bodies with no
headers is kept as open text.
Thread-level fields are flagged only when no email in the thread has them, since
replies often drop headers.

children.name: parse
children.doc:
Parse one Gmail thread.

Args:
    artifact: Raw Gmail document.

Returns:
    The thread with its emails and thread-level metadata.

children.name: messages_from_json_list
children.doc:
Format 1: the thread is a JSON list of email strings.

Args:
    content: Stripped Gmail document content.

Returns:
    One string per email, or None when the content is not a JSON list.

children.name: messages_from_python_list
children.doc:
Format 2: the thread is a Python list literal of email strings.

Args:
    content: Stripped Gmail document content.

Returns:
    One string per email, or None when the content is not a Python list.

children.name: messages_from_numbered_sections
children.doc:
Format 3: one `message_1_body:`, `message_2_body:`, ... section per email.

Also `messages_N_body`, `msg_N_body` and `mN_body`. Most of these emails carry
only their body, so sender, recipients and subject stay missing; a quoted email
inside a body that starts at a `From:` line is split off with its headers. These
read like group or company-wide mail: the sender is kept when a `From:` line
gives it, and missing sender, recipients or subject are not flagged.

Args:
    content: Stripped Gmail document content.

Returns:
    One string per email, or None when there are no numbered body sections.

children.name: messages_from_text
children.doc:
Format 4: plain text where each email starts at a `From:` line.

Args:
    content: Stripped Gmail document content.

Returns:
    One string per email, or None when there is no `From:` line.

children.name: message
children.doc:
Parse one email's leading header block, attachments and body.

A `-----Message 1-----` line before the headers is skipped.

Args:
    raw: Text of one email.

Returns:
    The email with whichever headers it has.

outline.name: string_list
outline.doc:
Accept a decoded thread only if it is a list of email strings.

Args:
    decoded: Value decoded from the document content.

Returns:
    The emails with newlines normalized, or None for any other value.

outline.name: split_addresses
outline.doc:
Split a header like `Ann <ann@x.com>, bob@y.com; Cy <cy@z.com>` into addresses.

Args:
    value: Header value.

Returns:
    The trimmed, non-empty entries.

outline.name: attachment_names
outline.doc:
Collect attachment file names from `Attachments:` lines and their bullets.

Only tokens that look like file names are kept, so prose around them and
annotations like `(PDF)` are dropped.

Args:
    raw: Text of one email.

Returns:
    The distinct attachment file names in order.

children.label: gmail.py (model)
children.summary: EmailThread and EmailMessage.
children.details: `EmailMessage` has sender, recipients, cc, date, subject, attachments, body and a `has_headers` property. `EmailThread` adds subject, participants, attachments (file names only; the dataset has no files) and messages.

outline.name: EmailMessage
outline.doc: One email with its headers; later replies often omit some headers.

children.name: has_headers
children.doc:
Tell whether the email carries any header.

Returns:
    True when it has a sender, recipients, a date or a subject.

outline.name: EmailThread
outline.doc:
An email thread with thread-level metadata collected from its messages.

Attachments are file names only: the dataset has no attachment files or paths.

children.label: GitHub
children.summary: Pull requests: description section plus parsed review comments.
children.details: 8,052 documents. The description is required (none means open text, 1 case) and is tried in seven section formats; review comments are tried in nine (`review_comments`, `conversation`, `discussion`, ...). Comments are parsed with `parse_comments(inline_speakers=True)`, because GitHub review conversations put several speakers on one line. Only a missing description is flagged; participants are the comment authors.

children.label: github.py
children.summary: GithubParser: seven description and nine review-comment section formats.
children.details: Each format is a static method that reads a differently named `key:` section through `section` from parsers/text.py (`description_section`, `pr_body_section`, `review_threads_section`, ...). `unlabeled_description` falls back to leading text. `parse` feeds the review text into `parse_comments`.

outline.name: GithubParser
outline.doc:
Parse a pull request: its description and review discussion.

The description and the review discussion appear under several section names,
one method each; the first one present is used. Only a missing description is
flagged: many pull requests have no review discussion, and that is left as None.

children.name: description_section

children.name: body_section

children.doc:

children.name: review_threads_section
children.doc:
Format 4: a `review_threads:` section.

    The section text, or None when the section is absent or empty.

children.name: review_discussion_section
children.doc:
Format 5: a `review_discussion:` section.

Args:
    text: Normalized pull request content.

Returns:

children.name: reviews_section
children.doc:
Format 6: a `reviews:` section.

    text: Normalized pull request content.

Turn a document stored as a Python list of strings into plain text.

Many Gmail threads are stored as the text of a list literal, one string per email,
written with `'` or `"` quotes as Python chose. The strings are decoded, which also
turns their escaped line breaks and quotes into real characters, and joined by blank
lines. Anything else, including text that only looks like a list, is returned as is.

Args:
    text: Raw document text.

Returns:

Returns:

outline.name: normalize_text
outline.doc:
Clean text for embedding without changing what it says.

Escaped line breaks and Unicode escapes are decoded, HTML entities are unescaped,
and Unicode is NFKC-normalized (non-breaking and other Unicode spaces become plain
spaces, full-width letters become normal ones). Invisible characters, control
characters, broken characters and emoji are removed, and typographic quotes become
plain ones. Runs of spaces inside a line shrink to one; indentation is kept.

Args:
    text: Raw text.

Returns:
    The cleaned text, stripped.

children.label: Chunk, embed, index
children.summary: Turns documents into chunks, vectors and a BM25 keyword index that retrieval searches.
children.details:
Produces the searchable data that retrieval reads: embedding rows in Postgres (pgvector tables, one per source type and vector size) and an on-disk BM25 keyword index.

Three entry points, each a CLI command:
- `train-rag ingest` runs `run_data_ingestion`: load, parse, normalize, chunk, embed, store, in batches of 500 documents.
- `train-rag index-summaries` embeds the summaries Fireflies, GitHub and Jira documents already carry.
- `train-rag index-bm25` tokenizes whole documents into a stemmed `bm25s` index under `data/bm25/`.

Documents come from the `documents` table loaded earlier (EnterpriseRAG-Bench loader); parsing and normalizing reuse the parsers and `processing/normalize.py`. Output goes to the retrieval modules, which search `embeddings` / `embeddings_768` and the BM25 folder.

Read `pipelines/data_ingestion.py` first, then `embedder.py`.

children.label: Embedder
children.summary: ABC that turns texts into normalized vectors; model classes are interchangeable.
children.details:
Contract: an `Embedder` has class-level `name`, `dimensions` and `max_tokens`, and one method `embed(texts) -> list[list[float]]` returning one unit-length vector per text, in order. Unit length means cosine distance ranks results.

A new model needs those three attributes, an `embed` that normalizes, an entry in `EMBEDDERS`, and a matching vector size in `tables/embedding.py` and a chunk size in `CHUNKERS` of the ingestion pipeline.

children.details:

- `GteModernBertEmbedder`: gte-modernbert-base, 768 dimensions, reads 8,192 tokens, runs in float16 with batch 4 and casts vectors back to float32.
- `EMBEDDERS`: maps the CLI names `minilm` and `gte` to the classes.

children.label: Strategy + registry
children.summary: Pipelines take any Embedder; EMBEDDERS maps CLI names (minilm, gte) to classes, and dimensions pick the table set.
children.details: Pipelines (`run_data_ingestion`, `index_summaries`) take any `Embedder` and never name a model. `EMBEDDERS` in `embedder.py` maps the CLI names `minilm` and `gte` to classes. The embedder's `name` picks the chunker in `CHUNKERS`, and its `dimensions` picks the table set in `EMBEDDING_TABLES` (384 -> `embeddings`, 768 -> `embeddings_768`), so switching models switches size, tables and chunk length together.

children.label: Chunk pipeline
children.summary: Resumable batch pipeline: load, parse, normalize, chunk, embed, store per document.
children.details:
The main path: documents are processed per source type in batches of `DOCUMENT_BATCH = 500`, each batch committed in one transaction.

Steps per batch: `load_documents`, `parse_documents` (parsed fields upserted to `parsed_documents`), `normalize_documents`, `chunk_documents`, `embedder.embed`, `store_chunks`. Before the first batch of a source the vector index is dropped; after its last batch `create_vector_index` rebuilds the StreamingDiskANN index.

Options: `sample` limits to the test sample (cited documents plus N distractors), `fresh` deletes the model's chunks first, `redo_lists` re-embeds documents stored as list literals. Progress is recorded for `train-rag progress-page`.

children.label: data_ingestion.py
children.summary: run_data_ingestion: plans pending documents and commits each batch of 500.
children.details: `run_data_ingestion` plans the pending documents per source type (`pending_documents`), then loops batches through the six steps. `CHUNKERS` holds a `RecursiveChunker` per model name. `forget_list_documents` deletes chunks of documents stored as a list literal so they become pending and are re-embedded from decoded text.

outline.name: forget_list_documents
outline.signature: (session: Session, dataset: str, embedder: Embedder) -> None
outline.doc:
Delete this model's chunks of the documents stored as a list literal.

Their chunks were made before normalization decoded such lists into plain text
(`decode_string_list`), so they were embedded as escaped list syntax. Without chunks
they count as pending again, and the run re-embeds them from the decoded text.

Args:
    session: Active database session.
    dataset: Dataset to fix.
    embedder: Embedding model whose chunks are deleted.

outline.name: run_data_ingestion
outline.signature: (embedder: Embedder, sample: int | None = None, fresh: bool = False, redo_lists: bool = False) -> None
outline.doc:
Ingest every document that has no chunks from this embedding model yet.

Args:
    embedder: Embedding model; its name picks the chunk size from `CHUNKERS`.
    sample: Only the test sample (every cited document plus this many random
        distractors), or None for the whole corpus.
    fresh: Delete this model's chunks first and start over.
    redo_lists: Re-embed the documents stored as a list literal (see
        `forget_list_documents`).

children.label: chunking.py
children.summary: RecursiveChunker cuts at paragraph, line, sentence, word, adding neighbour context.
children.details: `RecursiveChunker.split` cuts text at `SEPARATORS` (paragraph, line, sentence, space), recursing into pieces over `size`, and `merge` joins neighbours back up to `size`; a piece with no break left is cut hard at `size`. `chunks` prepends the title and adds `context` characters from the previous chunk's tail and next chunk's head (`tail`, `head`, cut at word boundaries). `chunk_documents` wraps the texts as `Chunk` models with a `position`.

outline.name: RecursiveChunker
outline.doc:
Splits text at the coarsest break that gives small enough pieces.

Text is cut at paragraph breaks first; a paragraph that is still too long is cut at
line breaks, then at sentence ends, then between words, and only as a last resort in
the middle of a word. Neighbouring pieces are joined back up to `size` characters.

Each chunk is then given a little context: the end of the chunk before it on top and
the start of the chunk after it at the bottom, so a chunk that starts mid-topic still

children.label: Neighbour context
children.summary: Chunks carry neighbour text so later steps can send a chunk with its neighbours, not whole documents, cutting LLM tokens.
children.details: Two kinds of neighbour context exist. Text: `RecursiveChunker.chunks` adds the tail of the previous chunk and the head of the next (100 characters for MiniLM) so a mid-topic chunk still says its topic. Links: `store_chunks` stores `previous_id` and `next_id` per row, so a retrieval step can send a hit with its neighbours instead of the whole document. The cost-savings article argues this cuts LLM tokens.

children.label: Retrieval
children.summary: Finds the documents for a query: BM25 and gte search, rank fusion, then a cross-encoder rerank.
children.details:
Turns a question into a ranked list of `RetrievedDocument` (doc id, title, best chunk, RRF score, rerank score) for the answering and evaluation code.

Flow of `RetrievalPipeline.run`:
- `normalize_text` cleans the query like the indexed text.
- `keyword_search` (BM25 over whole documents) and `semantic_search` (gte-modernbert over chunks, every source table at once) run concurrently, 50 candidates each.
- `reciprocal_rank_fusion` merges the two rankings.
- `describe` loads titles and chunk texts for the fused documents.
- `rerank` scores title plus chunk with a cross-encoder over the fused top 50 and the top `limit` are returned.

Data comes from the BM25 index on disk (built by `index_bm25`) and the pgvector embedding tables; results go to evaluation and the RAG answer step. The `Retriever` ABC in `retrieval.py` is the simpler synchronous API used for baseline comparisons. Read `pipelines/retrieval.py` first, then `fusion.py`.

children.label: Retriever
children.summary: ABC with retrieve(question, limit) and searchable_doc_ids(); EmbeddingRetriever and Bm25Retriever implement it.
children.details:
The contract every retriever shares: a class attribute `name`, `retrieve(question, limit)` returning one `SearchHit` per document, best first, and `searchable_doc_ids()` returning the dataset ids the retriever can find at all (used to score evaluation only on findable documents).

A new variant must set `name`, return at most one hit per document sorted best first, and make `retrieve` safe to call from several evaluation worker threads (the two implementations hold a `threading.Lock` around their shared model).

`distance` is lower-is-better in both implementations: cosine distance for embeddings, the negated score for BM25.

children.summary: Retriever ABC, EmbeddingRetriever (pgvector tables) and Bm25Retriever (bm25s index).
children.details:
- `Retriever`: the ABC.
- `EmbeddingRetriever(engine, embedder, field)`: finds which sources have embeddings of the field, embeds the question, queries each source table with `search_embeddings` for `limit * CHUNKS_PER_DOCUMENT` (5) chunks, then `best_per_document` keeps the closest chunk of each document.
- `Bm25Retriever(index_dir)`: loads a `bm25s` index and its `documents.json`, tokenizes the question with the same stemmer as indexing, returns whole-document hits with empty text; documents scoring 0 are dropped.

children.label: Interchangeable retrievers
children.summary: Strategy: both retrievers return SearchHit lists, so evaluation can swap them by name.
children.details: `Retriever` is a Strategy interface. `EmbeddingRetriever` (name `embedding`) and `Bm25Retriever` (name `bm25`) both return `list[SearchHit]` and expose `searchable_doc_ids`, so the evaluation code compares them with identical code. `Bm25Retriever` fits the shape by filling `field="document"`, empty `text` and `distance=-score`.

children.label: Locks around shared models
children.summary: A threading.Lock guards the embedder and stemmer because evaluation runs worker threads.
children.details: Both retrievers create `self.lock = threading.Lock()`. In `EmbeddingRetriever.retrieve` the lock wraps `embedder.embed` (one GPU model); in `Bm25Retriever.retrieve` it wraps tokenizing and `model.retrieve` because the stemmer object is shared. The inline comments say the evaluation's worker threads call them concurrently. The async pipeline uses an `asyncio.Lock` for the same reason (see RET.V1).

children.label: Hybrid pipeline
children.summary: Async BM25 + gte chunk search fused with reciprocal rank fusion, then described with title and chunk.
children.details:
Unlike the single-search retrievers, `RetrievalPipeline` runs BM25 and gte chunk search together and fuses them. It is async so many queries share one loaded embedder and index.

- `CANDIDATES = 50` documents are taken from each ranking; gte fetches `CANDIDATES * CHUNKS_PER_DOCUMENT` chunks per source table, then keeps each document's best chunk.
- `reciprocal_rank_fusion` with `RRF_K = 60`; gte is listed first so its best chunk describes the document.
- `describe` batches title and chunk-text queries per source.
- `run_keywords` is a BM25-only path for exact names, ids and rare terms.
- `RetrievalPipeline.load(rerank=False)` skips the reranker and returns the fused order.

On the full 511,962-document corpus the hybrid scored Recall@10 71.4% (article 002).

- `run(query, limit)` is the six numbered steps; with a reranker it fuses `RERANK_DEPTH` (50) documents, without one only `limit`.
- `keyword_search` and `semantic_search` use `asyncio.to_thread` for the blocking models; `search_source` queries one table per async session.
- `describe`, `load_titles` and `load_texts` attach title and chunk text.
- `rerank` builds `title\ntext` strings and sorts by score.
- `run_retrieval` is the one-shot helper used by the CLI.

children.label: Hybrid beats either search alone
children.summary: Equal-weight RRF of BM25 and gte lifts Recall@10 over each; the top 50 of each feed the fusion.
children.details: Article 002 reports that BM25 and gte miss different questions, so the pipeline takes the top 50 documents from each and merges them with equal-weight RRF. On the full corpus the hybrid reached Recall@5 62.9% and Recall@10 71.4%, about 3 points above the best single search at Recall@10. The article also notes the trade-off: the hybrid helps the top 10 but hurts the top 1 (41.7% Recall@1), which the reranker later repairs.
children.doc: docs/articles/002_first_retrieval_baselines.md

children.label: Async steps, one function each
children.summary: run() reads as numbered steps; blocking models run in asyncio.to_thread behind a model lock.
children.details: `run()` is annotated `# 1. Normalize` through `# 6. Rerank`, each step one small method. The blocking embedder and reranker run in `asyncio.to_thread`, and an `asyncio.Lock` (`model_lock`) serialises GPU use because concurrent queries share the models. Database work uses `AsyncSession` and `asyncio.gather` across source tables.

children.label: Cross-encoder rerank
children.summary: Reranker ABC and gte-reranker-modernbert scoring the title and chunk of the fused top 50.
children.details:
A second stage on top of the hybrid fusion. A cross-encoder reads the query together with a document's `title\nchunk` (up to 8,192 tokens) and returns a relevance score, which is more precise than comparing separate vectors but costs one model pass per document.

- `Reranker` ABC: `score(query, texts)` returns one float per text, higher is better, in input order.
- `GteModernBertReranker` loads `Alibaba-NLP/gte-reranker-modernbert-base` in fp16, batch size 4.
- Enabled by default in `RetrievalPipeline.load`; the pipeline sorts by `rerank_score`.

Article 002: reranking the top 50 lifted Recall@1 from 41.7% to 64.0% and Recall@10 from 71.4% to 78.8%, at about 3.7 s per question on a laptop GPU.

children.label: Evaluation
children.summary: Runs a RAG system over benchmark questions, grades answers with an LLM judge and reports metrics.
children.details:
Produces a scored report for one RAG system on the EnterpriseRAG-Bench questions, for whoever is comparing systems or tuning retrieval. `train-rag evaluate` runs a system plus a judge; `train-rag evaluate-search` measures retrieval recall alone with no LLM.

Flow of `evaluate()` in evaluate.py:
- load questions from the database (optionally one question type, a limit, or only those an earlier run got wrong)
- build the system and judge by name from registry.py
- `run_evaluation` answers and grades each question on a thread pool, stores the results in batches of 50, and returns a `RunSummary`
- print `format_report` and the Gemini cost line from `UsageMeter`

Questions and stored runs come from the repository/tables layer; the systems call the retrieval pipeline module (`RetrievalPipeline`) and Gemini. Read evaluation/system.py first, then pipeline.py.

children.label: RagSystem
children.summary: ABC: answer(question) returns a SystemAnswer; oracle and no-answer bound the scores.
children.details:
The contract every evaluated system shares: `answer(question: str) -> SystemAnswer`, nothing else. `SystemAnswer` carries the answer text, `retrieved_doc_ids` (best first), optional `cited_doc_ids` and an optional agent `trace`.

A new variant subclasses `RagSystem`, sets the class-level `name` and implements `answer`; then it is added to `SYSTEMS` in registry.py to be runnable by name. The system receives only the question text, never the gold answer or expected documents.

Two reference systems bound the scale: `OracleSystem` (gold answer and expected docs, should score near 100%, so any gap is judge noise) and `NoAnswerSystem` (always the not-found answer, correct only on info-not-found questions).

`ClarifyingSystem` is a subclass of `RagSystem` with `answer_with(question, person)`; `evaluate_question` in pipeline.py passes it a simulated `Person` from an optional `person_factory`. It is implemented in the separate CLAR module.

children.details: `RagSystem` is the ABC with the `name` ClassVar and abstract `answer`. `NOT_FOUND_ANSWER` is the shared refusal text used by all systems. `OracleSystem` is built from the questions and looks up the gold answer by question text; an unknown question gets the not-found answer. `NoAnswerSystem` ignores the question.

children.details:
Registered as `agent-rerank`. It first runs the same full-pipeline search on the question (counted as search 1), shows those top 5 documents to Gemini, then Gemini either answers or calls a tool: `search_knowledge_base` (the full pipeline with its own wording) or `keyword_search` (BM25 only, for exact names and ids). `MAX_SEARCHES = 3` counts the first one, so at most two more; once reached, function calling is switched to mode NONE and the next turn must answer.

Because it starts from the plain pipeline's result it can only add documents. `retrieved_doc_ids` is every document any search returned, in order found, and the full step-by-step `trace` is stored on the result.

The loop is built to be extended: `agent-snippets` (below) subclasses `AgentSystem` and overrides `tools`, `can_call` and `run_tool`.

The first search is automatic and counted in a `Budget` (searches, reads). Each tool call goes through the overridable `run_tool`, which returns the model's response and the documents found; a call past the limit gets an error (`LIMIT_REACHED`). `tools()` and `can_call(budget)` are hooks too, so `SnippetAgentSystem` subclasses it to change the tools and budget. `KnowledgeBase` is a Protocol with `retrieve` and `retrieve_keywords`, satisfied by `PipelineRetriever`. Tool declarations and trace steps now live in agent_tools.py. Prompts come from prompts.py. Searches are added to the `UsageMeter` at the end.

The first search and `search_knowledge_base` still return full document text (top 5). `keyword_search` returns 10 documents as short snippets: the lines matching the query with context, plus each document's id and length. children.label: evaluation/snippets.py
children.summary: Turns a document into the best matching passages for a keyword query.
children.details: `query_terms` tokenizes the query the way BM25 does (lowercase, stopwords removed, stemmed with the English Stemmer via `tokenize` from index_bm25). `matches` finds the words in a line that stem to a query term. `snippets` ranks lines by number of distinct query words then position, and shows up to `MAX_SNIPPETS` = 2, each with `CONTEXT_LINES` = 2 lines around it; a line over `LONG_LINE` = 500 chars becomes a 250-char window each side of the first match; lines already shown as context are skipped; with no match the first `FALLBACK_CHARS` = 300 characters are shown. `snippet_context` lays out one block per hit: number, source type, title, id, character count, then the snippets.

outline.doc:

chosen line is shown with `CONTEXT_LINES` around it, or, when it is longer than
`LONG_LINE`, as a window of `WINDOW_CHARS` around its first match. A line already
shown as another snippet's context is not chosen again.

Args:

    terms: The query's stemmed words.

Returns:
    Up to `MAX_SNIPPETS` passages, in document order.

children.label: Snippets save tokens
children.summary: Full documents cost the most tokens, so keyword hits are previewed and only chosen ones read in full.
children.details: The module docstring in agent_snippets.py states the reason: showing each keyword result as matching lines plus context lets the agent scan twice as many results (10 against top_k=5) for fewer tokens, then read by id only the ones that look right, within a separate budget of 3 reads. children.label: Training data for the embedder
children.summary: Builds synthetic training questions with hard negatives to fine-tune the embedding model.
children.details:
Produces about 2,000 train and 400 dev questions, each with its source document as positive and up to 5 hard negatives, so the embedder can be fine-tuned without touching the 500 benchmark questions (kept as a once-only test).

Flow, run through scripts in `exploration/training_questions/` (not files of this module):
- `sources.py`: picks source documents per type and source using the quotas, excluding the benchmark's right documents and their 20 nearest gte neighbours, dev first.
- `generate.py`: writes one question per document with DeepSeek via a small LangGraph, using the benchmark's prompts; answers are cleaned with `clean_question`.
- `mine.py`: searches (gte + BM25, RRF to 50), reranks with the source added, then applies `pick_negatives`; writes training_set.jsonl and dev_set.jsonl.

Read `quotas.py` first, then `drop_rule.py`. Uses the search and reranker from the retrieval modules.

children.label: Progress page
children.summary: Records how far long runs got in the database and shows the latest on a local web page.
children.details:
Produces a live view of the latest long run (ingestion pipeline or evaluation) for whoever is waiting on it.

Flow:
- A loop opens `RunProgress(engine, pipeline, total_items, ...)`, which inserts a `running` row into `pipeline_runs`.
- After each batch the loop calls `advance(stage, items, chars, note)`, which adds to the row's counters and bumps `updated_at`.
- On exit the row becomes `finished`, or `stopped` on an error or Ctrl+C.
- `train-rag progress-page` starts a FastAPI app on 127.0.0.1; `page.html` polls `/api/progress`, which returns the newest row as a `RunState` with elapsed and remaining seconds.

The module does not run anything itself; other modules (data ingestion, evaluation) import `RunProgress`. Read `recorder.py` first, then `latest_run_state` in the repository for the time estimate.

children.label: RunProgress recorder
children.summary: Context manager any loop uses to write per-batch progress to the pipeline_runs table.
children.details:
The contract every caller follows: build `RunProgress` with the engine, a pipeline name, the total item count, optionally total characters and a `unit` such as `documents` or `questions`; use it in a `with` block; call `advance(stage, items, chars=0, note=None)` once per finished batch.

It owns its own `Session`, so it does not interfere with the caller's transactions, and it is meant for one thread. There are no subclasses; a new kind of run only needs to call these two methods. Pass `chars` on every `advance` if `total_chars` was given, otherwise the character-based estimate will be wrong.

children.label: recorder.py
children.summary: RunProgress: advance() per batch, marks run finished or stopped on exit.
children.details: `RunProgress.__init__` calls `start_run` and keeps the stored row. `advance` calls `update_run` (commit per batch) and, at most once every `LOG_EVERY_SECONDS` (60), prints a line with the stage, done/total items and millions of characters left, plus the note. `__exit__` sets status `finished` when no exception occurred, else `stopped`, and closes the session; it does not suppress the exception.

outline.name: RunProgress
outline.doc:
Records how far a run got after every batch, in the `pipeline_runs` table.

The progress page (`train-rag progress-page`) reads it from there, so it works for a
run started anywhere. Any loop can report through it: count items (documents,
questions, ...) and optionally their characters, which give a better time estimate
when items differ in size. The run is marked `finished` when the block ends normally
and `stopped` when it ends with an error or Ctrl+C. A plain line is also printed once
a minute, for logs. Use it from one thread.

children.signature: (self, engine: Engine, pipeline: str, total_items: int, total_chars: int = 0, unit: str = 'documents') -> None
children.doc:
Set up the record of one run.

Args:
    engine: Database engine; the progress uses its own session.
    pipeline: Name of the run and its settings, shown on the page.
    total_items: Items this run will process.
    total_chars: Their characters, or 0 to estimate time by items alone.
    unit: What the items are, e.g. `documents` or `questions`.

children.name: __enter__
children.doc:
Start recording.

Returns:
    This progress record.

children.name: __exit__
children.signature: (self, exc_type: type[BaseException] | None, exc: BaseException | None, traceback: TracebackType | None) -> None
children.doc: Mark the run finished, or stopped when it ended with an error or Ctrl+C.

children.name: advance
children.signature: (self, stage: str, items: int, chars: int = 0, note: str | None = None) -> None
children.doc:
Count a finished batch.

Args:
    stage: What the run is working on now, e.g. the source name.
    items: Items in the batch.
    chars: Their characters, when the run counts them.
    note: Extra line for the page, e.g. the money spent so far; None keeps the
        current one.

children.label: Database as the channel
children.summary: Progress goes through the DB, so the page shows runs started in any process.
children.details: The recorder writes to `pipeline_runs` rather than calling the web app. The page process only reads the newest row (`latest_run_state`), so it can be started before, after or in a different process from the run, and it survives restarts of either. The cost is one commit per batch, which is small next to embedding or LLM calls. The docstring of `RunProgress` states this: 'so it works for a run started anywhere'.

children.label: Chars weigh the estimate
children.summary: Optional character counts improve the time estimate when items differ in size.
children.details: In `latest_run_state`, when `total_chars` is non-zero the speed is `done_chars / elapsed` and the time left is `(total_chars - done_chars) / speed`; otherwise it uses items. Documents vary widely in length, so counting items alone would mis-predict when long documents come last. Evaluation runs pass 0 characters and fall back to items per second.

children.label: Files
children.summary: The web app side of the module.
children.details: Only the reading side lives here: one Python file that builds the FastAPI app and serves the static `page.html` (not mapped as code). The recording side is the base.

children.label: page.py
children.summary: FastAPI app serving page.html and /api/progress, run with uvicorn on localhost.
children.details: `create_app` makes the engine, calls `create_tables` (so the page works on a fresh database), and registers `/` (returns the text of `page.html`) and `/api/progress` (returns `latest_run_state` or null). `serve_progress_page(port)` prints the URL and runs uvicorn bound to 127.0.0.1 only, so the page is not exposed on the network.

Returns:

Serve the progress page on this machine until stopped.

Args:

children.label: Also uses
children.summary: Run record model, table and queries.
children.details: The three layers (API model, SQL table, queries) that the recorder and the page share. They live outside the progress folder because the repo keeps all models, tables and repositories in their own packages.

children.label: models/pipeline_run.py
children.summary: RunState model returned by the API.
children.details: `RunState` is the pydantic shape sent to the page: ids and names, `status`, done/total items and chars, `note`, timestamps, `seconds_elapsed`, and `seconds_left`, which is None until a speed can be measured.

outline.name: RunState
outline.doc:
How far a run got and how much is left.

Items are counted in `unit` (e.g. documents or questions); `total_chars` is 0 for a
run that doesn't weigh its items by size. `status` is `running`, `finished`, or
`stopped` for a run that stopped updating without finishing. `seconds_left` is None
until the run has a measurable speed.

children.label: tables/pipeline_run.py
children.summary: PipelineRunRecord table.
children.details: `PipelineRunRecord` maps to table `pipeline_runs`. Character counts use `BigInteger` because corpora exceed 2 billion characters; timestamps are timezone-aware. A killed run keeps status `running`, so staleness is derived at read time.

outline.name: PipelineRunRecord
outline.doc:
One run of a pipeline or an evaluation, updated after every batch.

`total_items` is what this run had left when it started, counted in `unit` (e.g.
documents or questions); `done_items` counts what it has finished since. The
characters are optional (0 when a run doesn't weigh its items by size); when set, the
time left is estimated from them. `stage` names the step it is on, and `note` holds
any extra line for the page, such as the money spent so far. `status` is `running`
until the run ends; a run that was killed stays `running` but stops updating
`updated_at`.

children.label: repository/pipeline_run.py
children.summary: start_run, update_run, latest_run_state queries.
children.details: `start_run` inserts a row with stage `starting`. `update_run` adds items and chars, sets stage, status and optional note, and commits. `latest_run_state` picks the highest id, downgrades a `running` row older than `STALE_AFTER` to `stopped`, computes elapsed time (to now if running, else to `updated_at`) and the remaining time.

outline.name: start_run
outline.signature: (session: Session, pipeline: str, total_items: int, total_chars: int, unit: str) -> PipelineRunRecord
outline.doc:
Record the start of a run.

Args:
    session: Active database session.
    pipeline: Name of the pipeline and its settings, e.g. `data-ingestion gte`.
    total_items: Items the run has to process.
    total_chars: Their characters, or 0 to not weigh items by size.
    unit: What the items are, e.g. `documents` or `questions`.

Returns:
    The stored run.

outline.name: update_run
outline.signature: (session: Session, run: PipelineRunRecord, stage: str, items: int, chars: int, status: str = 'running', note: str | None = None) -> None
outline.doc:
Add a finished batch to a run.

Args:
    session: Active database session.
    run: The run, from `start_run`.
    stage: What the run is working on now.
    items: Items finished since the last update.
    chars: Their characters.
    status: `running`, or `finished` for the last update.
    note: New extra line for the page, or None to keep the current one.

outline.name: latest_run_state
outline.doc:
Describe the most recent run, with its elapsed and estimated remaining time.

The time left assumes the run keeps its average speed, in characters per second when
the run counts characters and in items per second otherwise.

Args:
    session: Active database session.

Returns:
    The run's state, or None when no run was recorded.

children.label: Stale runs
children.summary: A running row untouched for 5 minutes (STALE_AFTER) is treated as stopped or crashed.
children.details: A process killed with SIGKILL or a power loss never reaches `__exit__`, so its row stays `running`. Instead of a heartbeat process, `latest_run_state` compares `updated_at` with now: a run updates after every batch, at least every few seconds, so more than `STALE_AFTER` (5 minutes) of silence means it is gone. The page then shows `stopped` and no time left. A single very slow batch over 5 minutes would be misreported as stopped.

children.label: Storage layer
children.summary: Postgres storage: pydantic models, SQLModel tables and repository queries.
children.details:
The storage layer holds everything the other modules keep in Postgres (with the pgvector and vectorscale extensions): raw documents, parsed fields, benchmark questions, embeddings, evaluation results, pipeline progress and LLM-inferred data. It has no command of its own; it is imported by ingestion (`import_db.py`, `pipelines/data_ingestion.py`, `index_summaries.py`, `index_bm25.py`), retrieval (`retrieval.py`, `pipelines/retrieval.py`), evaluation (`evaluate.py`, `evaluation/pipeline.py`) and the progress page (`progress/`).

Each entity is split in three layers: a pydantic model in `models/`, a SQLModel table in `tables/` and plain query functions in `repository/` that take a `Session`. `database.py` registers every table on `SQLModel.metadata` and creates them.

Typical flow:
- `import_db.py` writes `documents` and `questions`.
- Ingestion reads documents, writes `parsed_documents` and per-source embedding tables.
- Retrieval reads embeddings through `search_embeddings` / `nearest_chunks`.
- Evaluation reads questions and writes `eval_runs` / `eval_results`.
- Long runs record progress in `pipeline_runs`.

Start with `database.py`, then `tables/document.py` and `tables/embedding.py`, which show the two main ideas: provenance-keyed documents and table-per-source vectors.

children.label: database.py
children.summary: Engine factories and create_tables for the Postgres schema.
children.details:
`database.py` is the shared entry point every other group depends on.

- `database_url()` reads `DATABASE_URL`, falling back to the local docker-compose database on port 5434.
- `get_engine()` gives the sync engine used by ingestion and evaluation; `get_async_engine()` gives the async psycopg engine used by the retrieval pipeline (`nearest_chunks`, `chunk_texts`, `document_titles`).
- `create_tables(engine)` runs `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vectorscale CASCADE` (which brings pgvector and the DiskANN index), then `SQLModel.metadata.create_all`, then one manual `ALTER TABLE`.

A new table only needs to be imported in `tables/__init__.py`; `database.py` imports that package for its side effect of registering the models.

children.label: database.py
children.summary: database_url, sync and async engines, create_tables with vectorscale
children.details: Imports `train_rag.tables` with `noqa: F401` purely so the table classes register on `SQLModel.metadata`. `create_tables` is called by the import and setup scripts before first use; it is idempotent. The vectorscale extension must exist before `create_all`, because the embedding tables use the `vector` column type.

Create an engine for the configured database.

outline.doc:
Create the vector extensions and every table that does not exist yet.

children.label: Manual migration
children.summary: create_tables adds eval_results.cited_doc_ids by ALTER because create_all never adds columns to existing tables.
children.details: `create_all` only creates missing tables, never adds columns to existing ones. When `eval_results.cited_doc_ids` was added (JSONB, NOT NULL, default `'[]'`), existing databases would have broken, so `create_tables` ends with `ALTER TABLE eval_results ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS cited_doc_ids ...`. There is no Alembic; any future column added to an existing table needs the same kind of line here. The `trace` column of the same table uses a `server_default` too but has no ALTER line.

children.label: Documents
children.summary: Raw dataset documents: table, queries and size model.
children.details:
Table `documents` (`DocumentRecord`) is the raw corpus: one row per source document, with `doc_id`, `dataset`, `source_type`, `title`, `content` (Text), `char_count`, `byte_size`, `source_file`, `row_index` and `loaded_at`.

`doc_id` is deliberately not unique, because the dataset reuses ids for near-duplicate documents with conflicting facts. Identity is the unique constraint `(dataset, source_file, row_index)`, so `insert_documents` uses `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and imports are repeatable.

Writers: `import_db.py` via `insert_documents`. Readers: `parsing.py` (`to_artifact`), `index_summaries.py` (`load_artifacts`), `index_bm25.py` and `pipelines/data_ingestion.py` (`load_documents`, `document_ids`, `bracketed_documents`), `sampling.py` (`sample_document_ids`, `ids_of_doc_ids`) and `repository/embedding.py` (`document_lengths`).

The models in this group (`Artifact`, `Corpus`, `CleanDocument`, `Chunk`, `DocumentSize`) are the in-memory shapes passed between loaders, parsers and chunkers.

children.label: document.py
children.summary: DocumentRecord: raw document row with provenance and size
children.details: `DocumentRecord` maps table `documents`. Columns `doc_id`, `dataset` and `source_type` are indexed; `title` and `content` are unbounded Text. `char_count` and `byte_size` are stored at load time. Other tables point at it through `documents.id` (`document_id` foreign keys in parsed, embedding and inferred tables).

outline.name: DocumentRecord
outline.doc:
One source document with its provenance and size.

`doc_id` is not unique: the dataset reuses a few ids for different documents
(near-duplicates with conflicting facts), so a row is identified by where it
came from instead.

children.label: document.py
children.summary: insert_documents, counts by source, document_sizes, get_document
children.details:
Query functions on `documents`:
- `insert_documents` does an idempotent bulk insert on the provenance key.
- `count_documents_by_source` groups counts by source type for one dataset.
- `document_sizes` computes chars and printed lines in SQL so text never leaves the database (escaped `\n` count as line breaks).
- `load_artifacts`, `load_documents`, `get_document` and `sample_artifacts` read rows back; `document_ids` and `document_lengths` return ids and sizes.
- `bracketed_documents` streams (with `yield_per`) documents whose text starts with `[` and ends with `]`, candidates for stringified lists.
- `sample_document_ids` picks a repeatable random sample from a seed; `ids_of_doc_ids` maps dataset ids to row ids.
- `to_artifact` converts a row to an `Artifact` that keeps `document_id`.

children.label: Parsed documents
children.summary: Typed fields parsers found, stored beside raw text.
children.details:
Table `parsed_documents` (`ParsedDocumentRecord`) stores what the parsers extracted from each raw document, next to the raw text: `document_id` (unique FK to `documents.id`), `doc_id`, `source_type`, `kind` (parsed model class name such as `SlackThread` or `OpenText`), `useful`, `flagged` and `data` (JSONB dump of the parsed model: participants, dates, channel and so on).

Sources with no parser (Google Drive, Confluence) have no row. `useful` is False for documents with too little text to index.

Writer: `pipelines/data_ingestion.py` via `upsert_parsed_documents`, which deliberately does not commit so the parse commits together with the chunks. The JSONB data is for filtering and linking documents later.

children.label: parsed_document.py
children.summary: ParsedDocumentRecord: parser output per raw document
children.details: `ParsedDocumentRecord` maps `parsed_documents`. One row per document (unique `document_id`); `kind`, `source_type` and `doc_id` are indexed. `data` is JSONB, `useful` and `flagged` are booleans set by the parser.

outline.name: ParsedDocumentRecord
outline.doc:
The parser's output for one raw document.

`kind` is the parsed model's name (`SlackThread`, `OpenText`, …); `data` is the
model dumped to JSON (participants, dates, channel and so on), for filtering and
linking documents later. Sources without a parser (Google Drive, Confluence) have no
row. `useful` is False for documents with too little text to index.

children.label: Embeddings and search
children.summary: Vector tables per source and size, with index and search.
children.details:
One embedding table per (vector size, source type), such as `slack_embeddings` (384 dimensions, MiniLM) and `slack_embeddings_768`. All share the columns of `EmbeddingRecord`: `document_id` (FK to `documents.id`), `doc_id`, `field` (`summary` or `chunk`), `position`, `previous_id` / `next_id` (neighbouring chunks of the same document), `model`, `text` and `embedding`. A document can therefore have many rows, per field, chunk and model.

Search is cosine distance on a pgvectorscale StreamingDiskANN index (`create_vector_index`, `drop_vector_index`).

Writers: `index_summaries.py` (`replace_embeddings`, `create_vector_index`) and `pipelines/data_ingestion.py` (`store_chunks`, `pending_documents`, `embedded_document_ids`). Readers: `retrieval.py` (`search_embeddings`, `embedded_sources`, `embedded_doc_ids`) and `pipelines/retrieval.py` (async `nearest_chunks`, `chunk_texts`, `document_titles`, `embedded_sources`).

children.label: embedding.py
children.summary: EmbeddingRecord base, Mini/Base variants, source_table factory
children.details: `EmbeddingRecord` is a plain SQLModel (not a table) with all columns. `MiniEmbeddingRecord` and `BaseEmbeddingRecord` fix the `Vector(384)` and `Vector(768)` types. `BASES` maps size to (class, table suffix). `source_table(dimensions, source_type)` creates the table class with `types.new_class`, and `EMBEDDING_TABLES[dimensions][source_type]` holds all of them, built at import time.

outline.name: EmbeddingRecord
outline.doc:
One embedded text of a document, with its vector.

A document can have many rows: per embedded field (`field`, e.g. `summary` or
`chunk`), per chunk of that field (`position`, 0 for a whole field) and per embedding
model (`model`). `previous_id` and `next_id` are the row ids of the neighbouring
chunks of the same document, None at its first and last chunk. `doc_id` is the
dataset id the benchmark questions cite; `document_id` links back to the raw document
row. The vector is searched with a pgvectorscale StreamingDiskANN index on cosine
distance.

children.summary: Store, delete, reserve ids, index and search vectors

Write side:
- `reserve_ids` takes ids from the table sequence in advance.
- `store_chunks` uses them with `neighbour_ids` to insert chunks that already know `previous_id` and `next_id`.
- `insert_embeddings` inserts in batches without committing.
- `replace_embeddings`, `delete_embeddings` and `delete_document_embeddings` remove then insert for a model and field.

Read side: `search_embeddings` (sync, cosine distance, returns `SearchHit` with text), `embedded_sources`, `embedded_doc_ids`, `embedded_document_ids`, `pending_documents` (documents not yet embedded) and `create_vector_index` / `drop_vector_index` (`USING diskann (embedding vector_cosine_ops)`).
